conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days since your baby arrived.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; we want you to feel completely safe and supported. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions at your pace, one by one.  

Shall we begin?  

**First question:** Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(small sigh)  
Lately… it’s mostly felt difficult. I’ll smile if something’s really silly, but that light, easy laughter I used to have—like with my partner or on a sitcom—just doesn’t come. Most of the week I’ve felt too tired or down to find things genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

(eyes drop to the blanket)  
I guess… I can still laugh a little, but it’s kind of forced. Most days it feels like work to even crack a smile, and the joy doesn’t stick around.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(shifts in the chair, voice quiet)  
Not really… I mean, I’ll plan little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the time comes I just feel flat. I go through the motions hoping it’ll feel fun, but the excitement I used to have just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

(nods slowly, eyes welling up)  
Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my mind jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I know logically it’s not all on me, but I still feel guilty almost every day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(hands twisting in lap)  
Pretty much every day. My thoughts just spiral—what if the baby stops breathing, what if I’m not doing enough, what if something awful happens—and I can’t always point to a real reason. I try to tell myself it’s just worry, but it keeps popping up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… like a wave of fear just hits me out of nowhere. My heart races and I feel shaky, even if the baby’s fine and nothing’s happening. It passes, but it’s happened a few times this week and it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely keeping my head above water. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep, worrying—everything piles up, and some mornings I just want to pull the blanket over my head. I still push through, but it feels overwhelming more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

(nods, rubbing tired eyes)

Yes… several nights this week I lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I might have done wrong or imagining worst-case scenarios about the baby. Even when she’s asleep, I can’t drift off for ages, and when I do I wake up again with anxious thoughts spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

(soft voice, eyes on the floor)

Most of the time, really. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this sadness sitting on my chest. Some moments are okay, but the happy feelings fade fast, and the gloom just settles back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. I’ll be feeding the baby or just sitting on the couch and the tears come. Nothing huge triggered it—I just feel so overwhelmed and low that crying sort of spills out before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(hesitates, voice drops to barely above a whisper)

Once or twice… just brief flashes, like “what if I weren’t here.” I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it—I’m too scared of leaving my baby—but the thought has flickered through, especially when everything feels too heavy.

I hear how heavy each day has felt since your baby arrived. You described forcing smiles, feeling emotionally flat, and carrying a constant weight of sadness on your chest. The worry spirals at night, the sudden panicky waves, and the tears that arrive without warning all sound exhausting. You also shared fleeting thoughts of not being here, and I want you to know these feelings are taken seriously and help is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is forced and joy is fleeting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports absence of anticipatory joy and describes feeling emotionally flat despite attempts to engage in activities, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily self-blame and guilt over routine infant behavior, indicating self-blame occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive, spiralling worries without clear triggers, matching 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of fear with physical symptoms happening "sometimes… a few times this week," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "more often than not," barely keeping up, and wanting to hide, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes most-nights sleep disruption driven by racing anxious thoughts, matching 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness "most of the time" with persistent heaviness and fleeting relief, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes spontaneous crying episodes multiple times this week without clear triggers, aligning with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places the patient well above the 14-point threshold for probable major depression; Item 10 score 1 mandates immediate safety review. She endorses daily <sym>depressed mood</sym>, near-total loss of pleasure, disproportionate guilt over infant care, nightly rumination-related insomnia, frequent tearfulness, and recurrent panic-type episodes, matching <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring anxiety. Passive suicidal thoughts, though without intent or plan, signal elevated risk requiring urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Implement continuous support person and remove firearms, medications, or other lethal means from home
3. Provide 24/7 crisis line numbers (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
4. Offer immediate evidence-based psychotherapy referral (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
5. Discuss short-term pharmacologic options compatible with breastfeeding if clinically indicated
6. Schedule follow-up within one week to review safety plan, medication adherence, and symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [___]  G[___] P[___]  Weeks post-delivery: [___]

Patient-reported symptoms (endorsed ≥ 5–6 days per week unless noted):

- Persistent low mood, sadness, “heaviness” (Q8)  
- Marked anhedonia—pleasurable activities feel “flat,” forced laughter (Q1–2)  
- Frequent crying spells without clear precipitant (Q9)  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt, self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive “worst-case” thoughts, nocturnal rumination (Q4,7)  
- Episodic panic-type sensations (palpitations, shakiness) without situational trigger (Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, difficulty coping with daily infant care (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia—initial and middle-night awakenings (Q7)  

Safety: Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I weren’t here”) reported once or twice this week; denies intent or plan.  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days × several weeks, causing distress and functional impairment (sleep, caretaking, social).  

Screening significance: High index of concern for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; rule-out post-partum anxiety disorder.  

Risk factors noted: Guilt, anhedonia, mood-congruent insomnia, passive suicidal thoughts.  

Plan: Score Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale; discuss further evaluation, supports, and safety planning today.
